seo.description: 20 High-yield JEE Main MCQ practice questions covering recoil of guns, spring buffers, rocket propulsion, Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, conveyor belts, falling sand carts, water jet reaction, and multi-stage rockets.

conceptCapsule.title: Variable Mass Dynamics & Practical Momentum Applications
conceptCapsule.summary: 1. Recoil Dynamics: In an isolated gun-bullet system, $m\vec{v}_b + M\vec{V}_g = \vec{0}$. If muzzle velocity $v_{\text{rel}}$ is relative to the recoiling barrel, absolute recoil speed is $V = \frac{m v_{\text{rel}}}{M + m}$. 2. Variable Mass Systems & Thrust: When mass is ejected at velocity $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}$ relative to the body, thrust force is $\vec{F}_{\text{thrust}} = \vec{v}_{\text{rel}}\frac{dm}{dt}$. For a vertically ascending rocket, $M\frac{dv}{dt} = u\left(-\frac{dM}{dt}\right) - Mg$. 3. Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation: In gravity-free space, $v - v_0 = u\ln\left(\frac{M_0}{M}\right)$. 4. Conveyor Belts: Adding mass at rate $\frac{dm}{dt}$ at constant speed $v$ requires an external pulling force $F = v\frac{dm}{dt}$ and power $P = Fv = v^2\frac{dm}{dt}$ (with $50\%$ converted to mechanical energy and $50\%$ dissipated as heat).
conceptCapsule.keyFormula: $$F_{\text{thrust}} = u_{\text{rel}}\left|\frac{dM}{dt}\right|, \quad v = v_0 + u\ln\left(\frac{M_0}{M}\right), \quad P_{\text{conveyor}} = \left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right)v^2, \quad V_{\text{recoil}} = \frac{m v_{\text{rel}}}{M + m}$$
conceptCapsule.examTrap: When sand drops vertically onto a moving horizontal cart, mass enters with zero horizontal velocity, exerting a drag force that slows the cart. Conversely, when sand leaks vertically out of a hole in the bottom of a moving cart, it leaves carrying the cart's instantaneous horizontal velocity ($v_{\text{rel}} = 0$). Thus, leaking sand exerts zero reaction force, and the cart's velocity remains constant!

questions.statement: A rifle of mass $4\text{ kg}$ fires a bullet of mass $40\text{ g}$ with a muzzle velocity of $800\text{ m/s}$ relative to the barrel[cite: 1, 3]. If the rifle is free to move, the recoil velocity of the rifle is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Let $M = 4\text{ kg}$, $m = 40\text{ g} = 0.04\text{ kg}$[cite: 1, 3]. The velocity $v_{\text{rel}} = 800\text{ m/s}$ is relative to the barrel[cite: 1, 3].
If the rifle recoils with speed $V$ backwards relative to ground, the velocity of the bullet relative to ground is $v_b = v_{\text{rel}} - V$[cite: 1, 3].
By conservation of linear momentum:
$$0 = m(v_{\text{rel}} - V) - MV \implies (M + m)V = m v_{\text{rel}}$$[cite: 1, 3]
$$V = \frac{m v_{\text{rel}}}{M + m} = \frac{0.04 \times 800}{4 + 0.04} = \frac{32}{4.04} \approx 7.92\text{ m/s}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A shell of mass $M$ at rest is fired from a gun of mass $M_g$[cite: 1, 3]. If the ratio of mass of the gun to that of the shell is $n$ ($M_g/M = n$), the ratio of the kinetic energy of the shell to that of the recoiling gun is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
From conservation of momentum: $M_g V_g = M v_s \implies V_g = \frac{M v_s}{M_g} = \frac{v_s}{n}$[cite: 1, 3].
Ratio of kinetic energies:
$$\frac{K_{\text{shell}}}{K_{\text{gun}}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} M v_s^2}{\frac{1}{2} M_g V_g^2} = \frac{M v_s^2}{M_g \left(\frac{v_s}{n}\right)^2} = \frac{M n^2}{M_g} = \frac{n^2}{n} = n$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A machine gun fires $360$ bullets per minute, each of mass $20\text{ g}$ with a muzzle speed of $600\text{ m/s}$[cite: 1, 3]. The average force that the gunner must exert on the gun to hold it in place is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Number of bullets per second $N = \frac{360}{60} = 6\text{ s}^{-1}$[cite: 1, 3].
Mass of each bullet $m = 20\text{ g} = 0.02\text{ kg}$, speed $v = 600\text{ m/s}$[cite: 1, 3].
Rate of change of momentum is the required holding force:
$$F_{\text{avg}} = N \cdot m \cdot v = 6 \times 0.02 \times 600 = 72\text{ N}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A cannon of mass $M$ mounted on a smooth horizontal surface fires a shell of mass $m$ with a velocity $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal barrel[cite: 1, 3]. The recoil speed of the cannon along the horizontal surface is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Relative to the barrel, the projectile's horizontal velocity component is $v_0 \cos\theta$[cite: 1, 3].
If the cannon recoils with horizontal speed $V$ backwards relative to ground, the horizontal speed of the shell relative to ground is $v_{sx} = v_0 \cos\theta - V$[cite: 1, 3].
Since no external horizontal force acts:
$$m (v_0 \cos\theta - V) = M V \implies V = \frac{m v_0 \cos\theta}{M + m}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A man of mass $60\text{ kg}$ stands on a trolley of mass $140\text{ kg}$ on smooth horizontal rails[cite: 1, 3]. The system is initially at rest[cite: 1, 3]. If the man jumps horizontally with a velocity of $4\text{ m/s}$ relative to the trolley, the absolute recoil speed of the trolley is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Let the trolley recoil with speed $V$ backwards[cite: 1, 3].
Speed of the man relative to ground is $(u_{\text{rel}} - V) = 4 - V$[cite: 1, 3].
By conservation of momentum in the horizontal direction:
$$m (4 - V) - M V = 0 \implies (M + m)V = m(4)$$[cite: 1, 3]
$$V = \frac{60 \times 4}{140 + 60} = \frac{240}{200} = 1.2\text{ m/s}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A gun of mass $100\text{ kg}$ fires a projectile of mass $1\text{ kg}$ with a speed of $400\text{ m/s}$[cite: 1, 3]. The gun recoils against a spring of spring constant $k = 4 \times 10^4\text{ N/m}$[cite: 1, 3]. The maximum compression of the spring is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Recoil velocity of the gun $V$:
$$M V = m v \implies V = \frac{m v}{M} = \frac{1 \times 400}{100} = 4\text{ m/s}$$[cite: 1, 3]
By conservation of mechanical energy for the gun and spring:
$$\frac{1}{2} M V^2 = \frac{1}{2} k x_{\text{max}}^2 \implies x_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{M V^2}{k}} = \sqrt{\frac{100 \times 4^2}{4 \times 10^4}} = \sqrt{0.04} = 0.2\text{ m} = 20\text{ cm}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A gun of mass $M$ fires a bullet of mass $m$ horizontally with speed $v$[cite: 1, 3]. The coefficient of friction between the gun and the horizontal ground is $\mu$[cite: 1, 3]. The distance travelled by the gun before coming to rest is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Recoil velocity of gun: $V = \frac{m v}{M}$[cite: 1, 3].
Deceleration of gun due to friction: $a = \mu g$[cite: 1, 3].
Using kinematic relation $V^2 = 2 a s$:
$$s = \frac{V^2}{2 \mu g} = \frac{(m v / M)^2}{2 \mu g} = \frac{m^2 v^2}{2 \mu M^2 g}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A rocket of initial mass $M_0 = 5000\text{ kg}$ is fired vertically upwards[cite: 1, 3]. The exhaust velocity of gases relative to the rocket is $u = 1200\text{ m/s}$[cite: 1, 3]. If the rocket is to have an initial upward acceleration of $20\text{ m/s}^2$, the rate of consumption of fuel must be ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Equation of motion of the rocket:
$$F_{\text{thrust}} - M_0 g = M_0 a \implies u \left(-\frac{dM}{dt}\right) = M_0 (g + a)$$[cite: 1, 3]
Given $M_0 = 5000\text{ kg}$, $u = 1200\text{ m/s}$, $a = 20\text{ m/s}^2$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$[cite: 1, 3]:
$$\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{M_0(g + a)}{u} = \frac{5000(10 + 20)}{1200} = \frac{5000 \times 30}{1200} = 125\text{ kg/s}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A rocket of mass $6000\text{ kg}$ is set for vertical firing[cite: 1, 3]. If the exhaust speed of its fuel is $1000\text{ m/s}$, the minimum rate of ejection of gas required just to overcome the weight of the rocket and hover is ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
To just overcome weight and hover:
$$F_{\text{thrust}} = M g \implies u \left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right) = M g$$[cite: 1, 3]
$$\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{M g}{u} = \frac{6000 \times 9.8}{1000} = 58.8\text{ kg/s}$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: In a gravity-free space, a rocket consumes fuel at a constant rate and ejects it with a relative velocity $u$[cite: 1, 3]. If the ratio of initial mass to final mass at burnout is $e^3$, the final velocity acquired by the rocket starting from rest is[cite: 1, 3]:
questions.solution:
Tsiolkovsky rocket equation in gravity-free space:
$$v = u \ln\left(\frac{M_0}{M}\right)$$[cite: 1, 3]
Given $\frac{M_0}{M} = e^3$[cite: 1, 3]:
$$v = u \ln(e^3) = 3u$$[cite: 1, 3]
Therefore, Option C is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: Sand drops vertically at a steady rate of $\mu = 5\text{ kg/s}$ onto a horizontal conveyor belt moving uniformly with a speed of $v = 2\text{ m/s}$[cite: 2, 3]. The additional power required from the motor to keep the belt moving at the same constant speed is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
The incoming sand has zero initial horizontal velocity[cite: 2, 3]. Rate of momentum imparted to the sand:
$$F_{\text{ext}} = v \frac{dm}{dt} = 2 \times 5 = 10\text{ N}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Power required by the motor $P = F_{\text{ext}} \cdot v$:
$$P = 10\text{ N} \times 2\text{ m/s} = 20\text{ W}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Note: Half of the total power supplied ($\frac{1}{2}\mu v^2 = 10\text{ W}$) increases the kinetic energy of the sand, and the other half is dissipated as thermal energy during sliding friction[cite: 2, 3].
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: An open cart of mass $M_0$ is moving horizontally with velocity $v_0$ on a frictionless surface[cite: 2, 3]. Sand starts falling vertically into the cart at a constant rate $\lambda\text{ kg/s}$[cite: 2, 3]. The velocity of the cart as a function of time $t$ is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
No external horizontal force acts on the system (cart + sand)[cite: 2, 3].
Total initial horizontal momentum is $P_x = M_0 v_0$[cite: 2, 3].
At time $t$, total mass is $M(t) = M_0 + \lambda t$[cite: 2, 3].
Since vertically falling sand brings zero horizontal momentum into the cart:
$$(M_0 + \lambda t) v(t) = M_0 v_0 \implies v(t) = \frac{M_0 v_0}{M_0 + \lambda t}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A cart of mass $M$ filled with sand of mass $m_s$ is moving with velocity $v_0$ on a frictionless track[cite: 2, 3]. Sand leaks vertically downwards through a small hole at the bottom at a constant rate $r = \frac{dm}{dt}$[cite: 2, 3]. The speed of the cart after all the sand has leaked out is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
When sand leaks vertically out of a hole, each particle leaves carrying the instantaneous horizontal velocity of the cart[cite: 2, 3].
Therefore, the relative velocity of the exiting mass with respect to the cart is zero ($v_{\text{rel}} = 0$)[cite: 2, 3].
The thrust force exerted is:
$$F_{\text{thrust}} = v_{\text{rel}} \frac{dm}{dt} = 0$$[cite: 2, 3]
Thus, the horizontal acceleration is zero and the speed of the cart remains constant at $v_0$[cite: 2, 3].
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A projectile of mass $3m$ is fired with an initial speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal[cite: 2, 3]. At the highest point of its trajectory, it explodes into two fragments of mass $m$ and $2m$[cite: 2, 3]. If the lighter fragment ($m$) falls vertically downwards immediately after explosion, the horizontal distance from the point of projection where the heavier fragment ($2m$) lands is: ($R$ is the original range)[cite: 2, 3]
questions.solution:
1. At the highest point, velocity is purely horizontal: $v_x = u \cos\theta$[cite: 2, 3].
Total horizontal momentum before explosion: $P_x = (3m) u \cos\theta$[cite: 2, 3].
2. Fragment $m$ falls vertically, so $v_{1x} = 0$[cite: 2, 3].
By momentum conservation: $$(2m) v' = (3m) u \cos\theta \implies v' = \frac{3}{2} u \cos\theta$$[cite: 2, 3]
3. Remaining time of flight is $t = \frac{T}{2}$[cite: 2, 3]. Distance covered from apex: $$x_2 = v' \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{3}{2} u \cos\theta\right)\left(\frac{u \sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{3}{4} R$$[cite: 2, 3]
Total distance from launch point: $X = \frac{R}{2} + \frac{3}{4}R = \frac{7}{4} R$[cite: 2, 3].
Therefore, Option C is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A flatcar of mass $M$ is initially at rest on a frictionless horizontal track[cite: 2, 3]. A man of mass $m$ runs from one end of the car to the other (length $L$) with a speed $u$ relative to the flatcar[cite: 2, 3]. The displacement of the flatcar relative to the ground during this process is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
Since no external horizontal force acts on the isolated system, the center of mass remains stationary[cite: 2, 3]:
$$\Delta x_{\text{cm}} = 0 \implies m \Delta x_{\text{man}} + M \Delta x_{\text{car}} = 0$$[cite: 2, 3]
Let the flatcar shift by distance $x$ backwards:
$$m(L - x) = M x \implies x = \frac{m L}{M + m}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A rifle on a frictionless horizontal table fires $n$ identical bullets of mass $m$ consecutively[cite: 2, 3]. The velocity of each bullet relative to the rifle barrel at the moment of firing is $u$[cite: 2, 3]. If the mass of the rifle without bullets is $M$, the recoil velocity of the rifle after all $n$ bullets are fired is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
When the $k$-th bullet is fired, the mass of the remaining rifle system is $M_k = M + km$[cite: 2, 3].
The velocity increment gained by the rifle from this shot is:
$$\Delta V_k = \frac{m}{M + km} u$$[cite: 2, 3]
Summing over all $n$ consecutive firings gives the total recoil speed:
$$V = \sum_{k=1}^n \Delta V_k = u \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{m}{M + km}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A jet of water from a nozzle of cross-sectional area $A$ strikes a stationary cart of mass $M$ horizontally with a speed $v_0$ and bounces off perpendicularly[cite: 2, 3]. Assuming no resistance, the acceleration of the cart when its speed becomes $v$ is ($ho = \text{density of water}$)[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
Relative velocity of water striking the cart when the cart moves at speed $v$ is $(v_0 - v)$[cite: 2, 3].
Rate at which water mass strikes the surface:
$$\frac{dm}{dt} = \rho A (v_0 - v)$$[cite: 2, 3]
Force exerted on the cart by momentum transfer:
$$F = \frac{dm}{dt}(v_0 - v) = \rho A (v_0 - v)^2$$[cite: 2, 3]
Acceleration of the cart:
$$a = \frac{F}{M} = \frac{\rho A (v_0 - v)^2}{M}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option B is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: In a rocket, to maintain a constant acceleration $a = 2g$ upwards in a uniform gravitational field $g$ where relative exhaust speed is $u$, the mass of the rocket must decrease with time according to the relation[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
Equation of motion for upward vertical flight:
$$-u \frac{dM}{dt} - M g = M a$$[cite: 2, 3]
Substituting $a = 2g$:
$$-u \frac{dM}{dt} = 3 M g \implies \frac{dM}{M} = -\frac{3g}{u} dt$$[cite: 2, 3]
Integrating from initial mass $M_0$ at $t = 0$ to $M(t)$ at time $t$:
$$\ln\left(\frac{M(t)}{M_0}\right) = -\frac{3gt}{u} \implies M(t) = M_0 e^{-3gt/u}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A bullet of mass $m$ moving with horizontal velocity $v$ strikes and gets embedded in a wooden block of mass $M$ suspended by a light string of length $l$[cite: 2, 3]. The minimum value of $v$ so that the block completes a full vertical circle is[cite: 2, 3]:
questions.solution:
By conservation of momentum during the rapid collision:
$$m v = (M + m) V \implies V = \frac{m v}{M + m}$$[cite: 2, 3]
For the combined block-bullet system to complete a vertical circular loop, the velocity at the lowest point must satisfy $V \ge \sqrt{5gl}$[cite: 2, 3]:
$$\frac{m v}{M + m} \ge \sqrt{5gl} \implies v_{\text{min}} = \left(\frac{M+m}{m}\right)\sqrt{5gl}$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].

questions.statement: A 2-stage rocket has total initial mass $M_0$[cite: 3]. The first stage has fuel mass $0.8 M_0$ and structural mass $0.1 M_0$[cite: 3]. The second stage has fuel mass $0.08 M_0$ and payload mass $0.02 M_0$[cite: 3]. The exhaust speed for both stages is $u$[cite: 3]. In gravity-free space, the final burnout speed of the payload starting from rest (discarding first stage structure before firing second stage) is[cite: 3]:
questions.solution:
Stage 1:
Initial mass: $M_{01} = M_0$[cite: 2, 3].
Mass after stage 1 burn: $M_{f1} = 0.1 M_0 + 0.08 M_0 + 0.02 M_0 = 0.2 M_0$[cite: 2, 3].
$$\Delta v_1 = u \ln\left(\frac{M_0}{0.2 M_0}\right) = u \ln 5$$[cite: 2, 3]
Stage 1 structural mass ($0.1 M_0$) is detached[cite: 2, 3].

Stage 2:
Initial mass: $M_{02} = 0.08 M_0 + 0.02 M_0 = 0.10 M_0$[cite: 2, 3].
Final mass (payload): $M_{f2} = 0.02 M_0$[cite: 2, 3].
$$\Delta v_2 = u \ln\left(\frac{0.10 M_0}{0.02 M_0}\right) = u \ln 5$$[cite: 2, 3]
Total final velocity: $$v_{\text{total}} = \Delta v_1 + \Delta v_2 = 2u \ln 5$$[cite: 2, 3]
Therefore, Option A is correct[cite: 1, 3].
